title: Crossed double treble — the tall X
subtitle: The same reverse-order method as the crossed treble, one step taller
excerpt: Crossed double treble works the same reverse-order logic as crossed treble but uses double trebles — taller stitches that create a more dramatic X shape and an airier openwork fabric. A Victorian open-lace staple.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776 — tall crossed stitch patterns in open lace. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Vol. 5 (1890) — crossed double treble in lace panels.

glossaryTerms.definition: Two double trebles worked in reverse order — skip a stitch, dtr into the next, then dtr into the skipped stitch passing behind the first — forming a tall X. Used in Victorian open-lace panels.

content.text: uses double trebles instead of trebles in the crossed-stitch method. The extra height makes the X shape more visible and creates a more open mesh — each pair of stitches spans a wider gap than the crossed treble version. It reads particularly well in lace-weight cotton or fine DK on a 4 mm hook.
Work to the two stitches where the cross will go.
Skip the next stitch. Yarn over twice and work a complete dtr into the stitch after the skipped one.
Yarn over twice and work a complete dtr into the skipped stitch — hook passes behind the dtr just made.
The two dtr cross. One crossed dtr pair made.

items.symptom: The cross is hard to form — stitches too close together
items.cause: Working on a hook that's too small for the yarn, making the stitches stiff
items.fix: Go up one hook size for crossed dtr to leave room for the stitch to reach back. The stitches need space to cross cleanly.

content.text: Crossed treble (the shorter version) is a good starting point if the dtr feels complex. In Victorian lace patterns, rows of crossed dtr alternate with rows of chains-and-clusters for full open-mesh fabric.
